issues.reason: The dangerous-keyword blocklist only does literal substring matching on single lines of files ending in lowercase .yml/.yaml. It can be bypassed in several ways: case changes (LOCALHOST), YAML flow or multi-line syntax, anchors and aliases, variables or templating (e.g. hosts: "{{ var }}"), other extensions (.YML, .json, included task files), or directives not on the list (connection: local). An uploaded playbook can therefore run arbitrary code on the controller/Celery host.

get_success_url returns the unvalidated `next` query parameter (or the Referer header), and form_valid passes it straight to redirect(), so a crafted link can send the user to an attacker-controlled site after password verification.

issues.reason: The blocklist only matches exact prefixes or bare names, so git's accepted abbreviated long options (e.g. `--upload-pa=cmd`, `--conf=core.sshCommand=...`) and underscore kwarg names (`upload_pack`, later dashified) get past the check and lead to arbitrary command execution in fetch/pull/push/clone.

The submodule path, which can come from an attacker-controlled .gitmodules during RootModule.update, is joined to the working tree without rejecting '../' segments. The submodule checkout can therefore be moved (and its .git file written) to arbitrary locations outside the repository.
The reference path supplied by the caller is joined onto the git dir without any ref-name validation, so names containing '../' (or absolute paths) can make it open files outside the repository.
The unvalidated traversal ref path becomes ref.abspath, and set_reference creates directories and writes the ref content there, allowing arbitrary file write outside .git.

The caller-supplied ref path goes through to_full_path, which does not reject '..' segments or absolute paths, and is then joined with repo.common_dir and passed to os.remove, so a traversal path can delete arbitrary files.
